question: Your CI reviewer is producing too many false positives. A teammate suggests adding 'Only report findings you are highly confident in' to the system prompt. Why is this unlikely to improve precision?
options: Claude has no calibrated confidence axis to filter on, so the instruction reduces volume but not the false-positive rate.
The instruction conflicts with Claude's safety training, which forces it to surface uncertain findings anyway.
Confidence-based filtering only works when paired with a temperature setting below 0.2.
It works, but only when wrapped in a tool_use schema rather than a text instruction.
explanations: Correct. 'High confidence' is not a quantity Claude measures against a held-out set; the instruction collapses into 'be slightly less verbose', which doesn't move the per-category FP rate.
Wrong cause — there is no safety override that forces uncertain findings to surface. The reason is the absence of a calibrated confidence axis.
Temperature affects sampling diversity, not whether 'high confidence' is meaningful as a filter; the instruction would still fail at temperature 0.
Wrapping the same vague instruction in a schema doesn't make 'high confidence' a measurable quantity; the structural problem is the criterion, not the format.

question: Which prompt fragment is the better example of an explicit categorical criterion for a comment-accuracy reviewer?
options: 'Be conservative when flagging comments. Only report comments you are confident are inaccurate.'
'Flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts the adjacent code's actual behavior; do not flag comments that merely paraphrase, omit edge cases, or use different wording.'
'Review all comments and report any that seem suboptimal, outdated, or unclear.'
'Examine each comment carefully and use your best judgement about whether it should be improved.'
explanations: Vague hedge with no decision boundary; this is the anti-pattern the topic warns against.
Correct. Names in-scope code shape (claim contradicts behavior) and explicitly excludes superficially similar shapes — the canonical structure of an explicit categorical criterion.
'Suboptimal/outdated/unclear' are adjectives, not categorical criteria; produces inconsistent classifications.
'Best judgement' is the maximally vague version of the anti-pattern.

question: A reviewer agent has five categories. Per-category precision is: SQLi 91%, null-check 78%, comment-accuracy 32%, dead-code 70%, naming 45%. PR authors auto-resolve the bot without reading. What is this phenomenon called?
options: Severity drift — the model is rebucketing findings between runs.
False-positive contagion — high-FP categories undermine trust in the accurate ones.
Recall collapse — the model is missing real bugs because of over-tuning.
Category leakage — findings are being attributed to the wrong category.
explanations: Severity drift is about inconsistent classification across runs, not about whole-channel trust loss.
Correct. The hallmark of contagion: aggregate looks acceptable but a noisy category trains reviewers to dismiss the channel, including findings from the accurate (91%, 78%) categories.
Recall collapse is a recall-side problem; here the issue is precision and reviewer trust, not missed bugs.
Category leakage is a labelling/attribution issue, not a trust issue.

question: Your severity rubric currently reads: 'Critical = severe issue, Major = important issue, Minor = small issue, Trivial = cosmetic'. Two runs over the same PR disagree on severities. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The model needs a higher max_tokens budget to reason consistently about severity.
Severity is defined by adjectives without code-shape anchors, so the model has nothing to apply consistently.
Temperature is too high; lowering it to 0 will fix consistency.
The rubric needs to be moved into a tool schema rather than the system prompt.
explanations: Token budget doesn't make ambiguous adjectives unambiguous.
Correct. Adjective-only rubrics ('severe', 'important') are ambiguous; the fix is concrete code-shape examples per level.
Lower temperature reduces sampling variance but cannot resolve a genuinely ambiguous criterion.
Rubric format isn't the issue; the criterion's vagueness is.

question: A category is firing at 35% precision while the team iterates on its criteria. A teammate argues 'leave it enabled in production — it occasionally catches a bug nobody else would have'. What is the strongest counter-argument?
options: Anthropic's terms of service require disabling categories below 50% precision.
Disabling avoids the cost of the additional API call.
Leaving it on causes the model to drift further; precision will degrade unless disabled.
Reviewers who have already disengaged from the channel don't read the rare correct finding either, so the practical recall of the noisy category is near zero.
explanations: There is no such ToS requirement; the reasoning is empirical, not policy-based.
Cost is a real but minor consideration; the dominant argument is trust.
Models don't 'drift' from being left enabled; this conflates with concept drift in supervised systems.
Correct. Trust loss is per-reviewer; once a reviewer auto-resolves the bot, even genuinely correct findings die in unread threads — so 'sometimes catches a bug' overstates the real-world recall.

question: Which of these is the best severity rubric for a CI code reviewer?
options: Critical / Major / Minor / Trivial — escalate based on the model's judgement.
P0 / P1 / P2 / P3 with a one-line description of impact for each level.
P0–P3 with a concrete code-shape example for each (e.g., 'P0: user-controlled input flowing into exec(...)' ; 'P3: style/comment tone — skip').
A single 'should-fix' boolean — let humans assign severity downstream.
explanations: Adjective rubric — the canonical anti-pattern; produces inconsistent classifications.
Better than adjectives but still description-driven; impact phrases ('would corrupt persistent state') are ambiguous without an anchor.
Correct. Concrete code-shape examples per level are the topic's prescription — they anchor classification consistently.
Removing severity altogether dumps the prioritisation problem on humans and forfeits the model's bucketing benefit.

question: An engineer says 'we'll fix the false-positive problem by emailing reviewers a reminder to read each finding carefully before resolving'. Why is this not a valid fix?
options: Reviewers will eventually comply if reminded weekly enough times.
Trust loss is structural and per-reviewer; you cannot patch a precision problem at the human layer — the fix has to be in the prompt criteria or by disabling the category.
The reminder only works if combined with a 'be careful' instruction in the system prompt.
Email reminders aren't logged in the audit trail required for ISO compliance.
explanations: Repeating a reminder doesn't restore trust once a reviewer has trained themselves to skim past the bot.
Correct. The topic's anti-pattern: precision problems must be cured at the prompt or deployment layer, never offloaded to humans.
Adding the same instruction in two places doesn't make it work; the precision problem is in the criteria.
Compliance/audit is an unrelated concern.

question: Which workflow correctly describes 'disable-and-iterate' for a high-FP category?
options: Lower the model's temperature for that category, monitor for one week, then decide whether to disable.
Remove the category from the active prompt; iterate offline against a labelled PR sample; re-enable only when offline precision clears the threshold (e.g., 85%).
Keep the category active but suppress its findings in the UI until precision improves.
Reduce the category's max_tokens to force the model to be more selective.
explanations: Temperature is not a precision dial; this leaves noise firing while you tune.
Correct. The exact disable-and-iterate workflow described in the topic.
Suppressing in the UI still causes the model to spend time on the category and risks accidental exposure; remove it from the prompt.
Token caps don't sharpen criteria; they truncate output.

question: Aggregate precision across all categories is 70%, which the team considers 'fine'. But developer trust has collapsed. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Aggregate precision is the wrong metric; one category is dragging trust down even though the average looks acceptable.
70% precision is below industry standard; the team should target 95% across the board before deploying.
Recall is too low — developers can tell the bot is missing findings they care about.
The bot's tone is too curt; developers need a friendlier UX.
explanations: Correct. Trust is per-reviewer, not per-aggregate; a single 35%-precision category at high volume can poison a 70% aggregate.
There is no universal precision standard; the issue is variance across categories, not the average.
Recall might also be a problem, but the symptom (collapsed trust under acceptable aggregate) points to FP contagion, not missed findings.
Tone may matter at the margin but doesn't explain a trust collapse under acceptable aggregate precision.

question: Which of the following is NOT a valid way to improve a noisy review category?
options: Rewrite the criterion to name in-scope code shapes and explicitly exclude similar-looking out-of-scope shapes.
Anchor each severity level to a concrete code-shape example.
Disable the category in production while iterating offline.
Lower the temperature so the model is 'more cautious' and produces fewer findings.
explanations: Valid — this is the canonical structural fix.
Valid — concrete code-shape examples are the prescribed severity anchor.
Valid — disable-and-iterate is the correct workflow when criteria aren't yet sharp.
Correct (the invalid option). Temperature affects sampling diversity, not the criteria the model applies; noise stays noisy. The topic explicitly calls this out as an anti-fix.

question: Your Claude Code reviewer has a 'comment accuracy' category at 32% precision. Engineering leadership wants the lowest-risk move that restores developer trust this sprint. What do you do?
options: Disable the comment-accuracy category in the production prompt; iterate offline against labelled PRs; re-enable only after offline precision clears 85%.
Add 'be conservative when flagging comments' to the system prompt and monitor for one week.
Increase the severity threshold so only 'critical' comment findings surface.
Have a human review every comment-accuracy finding before it posts to the PR.
explanations: Correct. Disable-and-iterate is the standard remediation: stop firing noise, sharpen criteria offline, re-enable on a precision threshold.
Vague hedges don't move the FP rate; trust will keep eroding for another week.
There is no 'severity threshold' that filters a poorly-defined category — severities are buckets within a criterion, not a precision filter.
Adds a human bottleneck and doesn't fix the underlying criterion; the moment the human falls behind, the noise returns.

question: Which severity rubric is most likely to produce consistent classifications across runs?
options: Critical, Major, Minor, Trivial — defined as 'most severe' down to 'least severe'.
P0 = blocks merge; P1 = needs change; P2 = nice-to-have; P3 = skip.
P0–P3 each anchored with a one-line code-shape example (e.g., 'P0: user input flowing into exec(...)' ; 'P2: dead branch like if (x) return x; return x;').
A continuous severity score 0.0–1.0 reported as a confidence value alongside each finding.
explanations: Pure adjective rubric — the canonical inconsistent shape.
Description-only rubric; 'needs change' and 'nice-to-have' are still adjective-equivalents and produce drift.
Correct. Code-shape anchors per level are what the topic prescribes for consistent classification.
Self-reported confidence/severity scores are poorly calibrated; the topic warns against confidence-based axes.

question: Per-category precision: SQLi 91%, null-check 78%, comment-accuracy 32%. Aggregate: 67%. PR authors are dismissing the entire bot. Which action best preserves the value of the SQLi category?
options: Disable comment-accuracy in production immediately; keep SQLi and null-check firing; sharpen comment-accuracy offline.
Lower the temperature globally so the model is more cautious across all categories.
Tell the bot to label SQLi findings as '[HIGH-PRIORITY]' so reviewers see them first.
Switch to a more capable model so all categories converge at higher precision.
explanations: Correct. The trust signal is per-channel; removing the contagious category restores attention to the precise ones.
Temperature is not a precision dial; this won't restore trust in any category.
Labels don't fix trust loss — reviewers who auto-resolve don't read the labels either.
Model swaps may help the disabled category eventually but don't address the immediate trust collapse.

question: Which prompt change is the strongest fix for 'the model keeps flagging terse but accurate comments as inaccurate'?
options: Add 'Be conservative — only flag comments you are highly confident are wrong.'
Add a confidence-score self-report and filter findings below 0.8.
Lower the model's temperature to 0 so it's deterministic.

Replace the criterion with: 'Flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts the adjacent code's actual behavior. Do not flag comments that merely paraphrase, omit edge cases, or are terser than ideal.'
explanations: Vague hedge — fails to specify which shapes are out of scope; terse comments will keep getting flagged.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the model is already 'confidently wrong' on these findings.
Temperature 0 makes outputs reproducible but doesn't change what the criterion considers an inaccurate comment.
Correct. Names the in-scope shape (claim contradicts behavior) and explicitly excludes 'terse but accurate' as out of scope.

question: An engineer proposes: 'Let's keep the noisy category live but add a banner above each PR saying "please read the bot's findings carefully."' Why won't this restore trust?
options: Banners aren't supported by GitHub's PR UI.

Trust loss is structural — once reviewers have learned to dismiss the channel, prompting them to 'read carefully' doesn't reverse the conditioning; the fix has to be in the prompt or by disabling the category.
It will restore trust, but only after 4–6 weeks of consistent banner display.
The banner conflicts with the team's CONTRIBUTING.md guidelines.
explanations: GitHub PR UI capabilities aren't the issue.
Correct. Patching at the human layer is the topic's anti-pattern; trust must be restored by changing the bot's output, not by exhorting reviewers.
There is no evidence such an effect exists; the topic explicitly rejects human-layer fixes.
Style-guide alignment isn't the substantive objection.

question: Which of the following is the clearest example of false-positive contagion?
options: A reviewer's null-check category drifts from 80% to 65% precision over a quarter.
Two categories both have 70% precision; reviewers complain about both equally.
One category at 30% precision drowns the channel; reviewers stop reading even the 92%-precise SQLi findings.
The bot misses a real bug in a critical PR.
explanations: That's drift in a single category, not contagion across categories.
Equal complaints proportional to precision is normal triage, not contagion.
Correct. Contagion is the cross-category trust collapse triggered by one noisy category.
A miss is a recall problem, not a precision/contagion problem.

question: Your team adds 'only report high-confidence findings' to the system prompt and observes a 30% drop in finding volume. False-positive *rate* is unchanged. What's the best interpretation?
options: The instruction is starting to work; precision will improve over the next week.
Volume reduction without rate improvement is the predicted outcome of vague hedges — the model produced fewer findings but didn't change the criterion, so the FP rate is structurally the same.
The model is sandbagging — it could be more precise but is being lazy.
Volume drop indicates the model has lost calibration and needs retraining.
explanations: Vague hedges don't 'kick in' over time; the criterion is unchanged.
Correct. The topic predicts exactly this: hedge instructions reduce volume non-uniformly, leaving the per-category FP rate untouched.
Anthropomorphising; the model isn't withholding effort.
Models don't lose calibration from prompt instructions; this misuses ML terminology.

question: Which of these is a valid reason to PREFER explicit categorical criteria over a confidence-score-based filter?
options: Categorical criteria are cheaper because they use fewer tokens than confidence scores.
LLM self-reported confidence scores are poorly calibrated; categorical criteria define a decision boundary the model can apply consistently.
Confidence scores are not supported by the Anthropic API for tool calls.
Categorical criteria automatically reduce temperature, which improves consistency.
explanations: Token cost is not the principled reason.
Correct. The topic's central argument: confidence is not a calibrated axis the model can filter on, but a categorical decision boundary is something the model can apply turn after turn.
Confidence scores can be requested via tool schemas; the API doesn't block them. The issue is calibration, not support.
Criteria don't change temperature; this conflates concepts.

question: Which severity-level definition is most exam-aligned for a P0 'block-merge' bucket?
options: P0 = a critical issue that must be fixed before merge.
P0 = an issue with severe security or correctness implications.
P0 = user-controlled input flowing into shell/SQL/template execution without sanitisation, e.g., `exec('ls ' + req.body.path)`.
P0 = an issue the bot is highly confident about.
explanations: Adjective-driven; produces inconsistent classifications.
Description-only; 'severe' is still ambiguous.
Correct. Concrete code-shape example anchors P0 consistently — the topic's prescription.
Confidence-based; the topic explicitly rejects this axis.

question: A team's reviewer is at 70% aggregate precision but trust has collapsed. Per-category data is unavailable. What's the highest-leverage diagnostic step?
options: Lower the model's temperature and re-measure aggregate precision.
Switch to a larger model and re-measure.
Compute per-category precision; identify the worst category and check whether disabling it would restore aggregate trust signal.
Add 'be conservative' to the prompt and re-measure aggregate precision.
explanations: Doesn't diagnose anything; doesn't reveal the contagious category.
Doesn't diagnose; treats a measurement gap as a model gap.
Correct. Aggregate hides contagion; per-category breakdown is the diagnostic the topic prescribes.
Hedges don't diagnose and don't fix the rate; aggregate may even drop while contagion persists.

question: Your reviewer flags many minor formatting issues and obscures the occasional security finding. The team wants the simplest prompt-only fix. What's the strongest move?
options: Add 'do not flag formatting issues' as a single bullet at the end of the system prompt.
Anchor severities with code-shape examples, with formatting/style explicitly placed in a default-skip P3 bucket.
Lower temperature to 0 to reduce 'creative' findings.
Ask the model to self-report a confidence score and filter below 0.8.
explanations: A single negation may help slightly but doesn't establish the severity structure that prevents future drift; brittle.
Correct. Severity anchored by code-shape with a default-skip bucket for formatting is the topic's prescribed structural fix.
Temperature isn't a precision dial.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; doesn't address the criterion.

question: After disabling a high-FP category, the team is iterating offline. What is the correct re-enable criterion?
options: Re-enable when the category has been disabled for two weeks, regardless of offline precision.
Re-enable as soon as the criteria have been edited in the prompt.
Re-enable only when offline precision on a labelled sample clears a pre-set threshold (commonly 80–90%).
Re-enable after a single successful run on one labelled PR.
explanations: Time alone doesn't measure precision; this trades waiting for measurement.
Editing the prompt without measuring offline precision is precisely the gap the topic warns against.
Correct. The disable-and-iterate workflow re-enables on an offline precision threshold against a labelled sample.
A single PR isn't a labelled sample; one run is noise, not signal.

question: An engineer argues 'aggregate precision is what matters — categories are an internal detail'. Which counter-argument is most exam-aligned?
options: Aggregate precision is the right metric; the engineer is correct.
Aggregate precision is meaningless because it averages over arbitrary buckets.
Trust is per-reviewer/per-channel; one noisy category at high volume can poison a healthy aggregate, so per-category precision is the actionable metric.
Aggregate precision should be replaced with recall, since recall correlates with developer satisfaction.
explanations: The engineer is wrong precisely because of contagion.
Aggregate isn't meaningless — it's just hiding within-channel variance that drives trust.
Correct. Per-category precision is the metric the topic prescribes for diagnosing and preventing contagion.
Recall and precision both matter; replacing one ambiguity with another isn't the fix.

question: Two valid prompt fixes are: (a) sharpen the criterion with explicit categorical criteria, (b) anchor severities with code-shape examples. A third proposed fix is 'lower temperature for the noisy category only'. Why is (c) wrong even though it sounds plausible?
options: Per-category temperature isn't supported by the Anthropic API, so the proposal is impossible.
Temperature controls sampling diversity, not the criteria the model applies; lower temperature makes the noise more reproducible, not less noisy.
Lowering temperature suppresses real findings disproportionately, hurting recall.
Temperature must always be set globally; per-category overrides aren't a coherent concept.
explanations: API-feature objections sidestep the principle.
Correct. The topic's anti-pattern: temperature is not a precision dial; the criterion is what determines precision.
Recall might suffer too, but the principled objection is that temperature doesn't address the criterion.
Conceptual point about scope, not the underlying reason temperature fails as a precision tool.

question: Which of these symptoms most strongly suggests a 'criterion problem' rather than a 'model capability problem'?
options: The reviewer misses subtle race conditions that require deep cross-file reasoning.
The reviewer flags many comments as 'inaccurate' that are merely terse rephrasings of the code's behavior.
The reviewer's findings vary in length depending on the PR size.
The reviewer is slower on PRs with more than 10 files.
explanations: Cross-file reasoning misses are typically capability/context-window issues, not criterion issues.
Correct. Terse-but-accurate comments being flagged is exactly the criterion problem the topic targets — the criterion fails to exclude paraphrase/terseness.
Output length variance is a stylistic artefact, not a criterion issue.
Latency is an infra/orchestration issue, not a criterion issue.

question: Your team wants to A/B test 'be conservative' against 'explicit categorical criteria' on the same review category. Which outcome would the topic predict?
options: Both arms reduce volume; only the explicit-criteria arm reduces the false-positive *rate*.
The 'be conservative' arm wins on precision because Claude responds well to natural-language hedging.
Both arms produce identical metrics because the prompts mean the same thing.
The explicit-criteria arm reduces recall to near-zero because it's too restrictive.
explanations: Correct. The topic's empirical claim: hedges reduce volume but not rate; explicit criteria are the structural fix that moves the rate.
Claude does not 'respond' to hedging in a calibrated way; the topic explicitly rejects this.
The two prompts mean very different things — one is vague, one is structural.
Explicit criteria are scoped, not necessarily restrictive; the prediction is improved precision, not destroyed recall.

question: An engineer says: 'I added five examples of bad findings to the prompt as a few-shot block; precision improved from 30% to 80%.' Why is this consistent with the topic's principles?
options: Few-shot examples bypass the model's calibration, which is normally locked.
Concrete examples function as anchors that establish a categorical decision boundary, which is what the topic prescribes — they're a form of explicit criterion.
Few-shot prompting changes the model's internal confidence threshold.
Examples are what trigger the model's 'be careful' mode.
explanations: There is no 'locked calibration' to bypass; this is mechanistically wrong.
Correct. Examples make the criterion concrete and consistent — the same role code-shape examples play in severity rubrics.
Few-shot doesn't manipulate a confidence threshold; it shapes the decision boundary by example.
There is no internal 'be careful' mode.

question: Your reviewer is firing hundreds of 'naming convention' findings per PR, each one technically defensible. Developer trust is collapsing. Most exam-aligned fix?
options: Disable the naming-convention category in production; if naming review is required, sharpen the criterion offline (e.g., 'flag a name only when it directly conflicts with a documented convention') and re-enable on a precision threshold.
Add 'limit naming-convention findings to 5 per PR' to the system prompt.
Tell the bot to phrase naming findings more politely.
Lower temperature so the bot is less inclined to nitpick.
explanations: Correct. The exact disable-and-iterate move; volume-driven contagion is one of the canonical reasons to disable.
Caps suppress symptoms but don't address that the criterion is too broad; contagion continues at lower volume.
Tone doesn't restore trust once reviewers have disengaged.
Temperature isn't a precision dial.

question: Why is 'flag a comment only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior' a stronger criterion than 'flag inaccurate comments'?
options: It uses fewer tokens.
It names a specific code shape (claim vs behavior contradiction) the model can detect, which excludes paraphrase, terseness, and tone — categories the vague version would sweep in.
It triggers Claude's structured-output mode, which has higher precision.
It contains the word 'only', which Claude weights more heavily than other words.
explanations: Token count is incidental.
Correct. Naming the in-scope shape and implicitly excluding similar-looking out-of-scope shapes is the structural property of an explicit criterion.
There is no 'structured-output mode' triggered by a phrasing.
Word-weighting folklore.

question: Which of these is the WEAKEST argument for keeping a 35%-precision category live in production?
options: It occasionally catches a real bug nobody else would.
Disabling categories looks bad on the team's roadmap.
Disabling means we'll never find that 35% of real bugs.
Reviewers will eventually learn to triage the noise.
explanations: A weak argument, but not the weakest — at least it appeals to recall.
A non-technical political argument — weak but honest.
Mathematically wrong: 35% is precision, not recall — it doesn't mean 35% of real bugs are found.
Correct (the weakest). Asks reviewers to absorb the noise — patching at the human layer, which is the topic's explicit anti-pattern, and reviewers in practice disengage rather than triage harder.

question: A staff engineer argues: 'lowering temperature to 0 effectively gives us deterministic precision — same input, same output, so the FP rate is bounded by the criterion.' Why does this miss the point of the topic?
options: Determinism doesn't fix the criterion; if the criterion is vague, the model deterministically produces noise. Reproducibility is orthogonal to precision.
Temperature 0 is not actually deterministic across model versions, so the argument is unsound on its own terms.
Temperature 0 increases hallucinations because the model can't sample alternative completions.
Anthropic's API doesn't support temperature 0; only 0.1 minimum.
explanations: Correct. The deepest critique: a deterministic noisy reviewer is still a noisy reviewer. Temperature affects sampling variance, not the criterion that drives precision.
Tangentially true but not the principled point.
Hallucinations don't increase at low temperature in the way described.
Temperature 0 is supported.

question: Two prompts are proposed to fix a noisy security reviewer. Prompt A: 'flag XSS only when user-controlled input flows into innerHTML/document.write/dangerouslySetInnerHTML without sanitisation; do not flag innerHTML use on static strings or sanitised input'. Prompt B: 'be highly precise on XSS findings, only report ones you are confident in'. Per the topic, which is stronger and why?
options: B, because it appeals to the model's calibrated confidence, which is robust at production scale.

A, because it names in-scope code shapes (user input flowing into specific sinks) AND explicitly excludes similar-looking out-of-scope shapes (static or sanitised inputs) — a categorical decision boundary the model can apply consistently.
Equally strong — they communicate the same intent in different words.
B, because shorter prompts always outperform longer ones.
explanations: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the topic explicitly rejects this axis.
Correct. Naming the in-scope sinks and explicitly excluding sanitised/static cases is the canonical structure of an explicit categorical criterion.
They differ structurally — A defines a decision boundary, B is a hedge.
Length isn't the metric; structural specificity is.

question: Your team observes that the reviewer is 90% precise on PRs from the platform team but 40% precise on PRs from the experiments team. Same prompt, same model. What's the most exam-aligned diagnosis?
options: The criteria likely match platform-team idioms but are too broad for the experiments team's code patterns; sharpen criteria to be team-agnostic, or accept that one criterion may not fit both codebases and fork the prompt.
The model is biased against the experiments team for non-technical reasons.
Temperature drift between teams.
The experiments team's PRs are inherently noisier; nothing can be done.
explanations: Correct. The criterion is mismatched to one codebase's idioms — the structural fix is sharpening the criterion or splitting it, not asking reviewers to triage harder.
Anthropomorphic; not a useful diagnosis.
Temperature is per-call, not per-team.
Defeatist and not the topic's prescription; criteria can be sharpened or scoped.

question: A 'comment-accuracy' category has been disabled in production for two weeks. Offline precision on the latest labelled sample is 67%. Should the team re-enable?
options: Yes — two weeks is the standard cooldown.
Yes — 67% is above the 50% bar.
No — re-enable only when offline precision clears the pre-set threshold (commonly 80–90%); 67% is below the bar and would re-introduce contagion.
Yes — disabled categories can't be improved further; re-enabling is the only way to gather more signal.
explanations: Time isn't the gating criterion.
There's no rationale for 50% — re-enabling at that level would re-introduce contagion.
Correct. Disable-and-iterate re-enables on a precision threshold against a labelled sample, not on time or improvement direction.
Wrong — offline iteration against a labelled sample is exactly how to keep improving without re-enabling.

question: Reviewing a system prompt, you see this severity rubric: 'P0: would corrupt persistent state. P1: would degrade user experience. P2: would waste developer time.' Why is this still problematic per the topic?
options: It uses 'P' nomenclature instead of 'critical/major/minor' — the model prefers verbal labels.
It has too few levels; production needs at least five.
Each level is defined by impact phrases that are themselves ambiguous ('persistent state', 'degrade UX'); without code-shape examples per level, classification will still drift across runs.
Severity rubrics shouldn't appear in system prompts at all — they belong in tool schemas.
explanations: Naming convention isn't the issue.
Number of levels isn't the issue.
Correct. Replacing adjectives with impact phrases is an improvement but still leaves ambiguity; the topic prescribes concrete code-shape examples per level for consistent classification.
Severity rubrics in system prompts are fine; the issue is anchoring.

question: Engineering leadership is convinced that 'recall is everything — better to flag 10 false positives than miss 1 real bug'. Per the topic, what is the strongest pushback?
options: Recall and precision are equally important; the leadership statement is balanced.
Once reviewers disengage from a noisy channel, effective recall on the channel approaches zero — so prioritising raw recall over precision destroys the very recall it's trying to protect.
Recall is irrelevant; only precision matters in code review.
The right balance is set by the model, not by the team.
explanations: Doesn't address the asymmetry the topic highlights.
Correct. The topic's deepest point: trust is the gating resource — a high-recall, low-precision reviewer that nobody reads has effective recall of zero, dominating any recall gain.
Recall obviously matters — the topic doesn't reject it; it argues precision protects effective recall.
Hand-waves the question.

question: Which of these is the MOST subtle anti-fix for a noisy review category — i.e., one that sounds principled but doesn't actually move per-category precision?
options: Adding 'be conservative' to the system prompt.
Lowering temperature to 0.
Switching to a larger model.
Asking the model to self-report a confidence score per finding and filtering below a threshold.
explanations: Obvious anti-fix — a vague hedge.
Obvious anti-fix once you know temperature isn't a precision dial.
Larger models may help marginally but don't address vague criteria; medium-subtle.

Correct (most subtle). Self-reported confidence sounds principled but is poorly calibrated; the topic explicitly rejects confidence-based filtering as a precision tool, and many engineers reach for it because it sounds quantitative.

question: Your reviewer's 'naming convention' category fires 200 findings per PR, each technically correct against your style guide. Aggregate precision is therefore 100% by audit, yet developers ignore the bot. What's happening, per the topic?
options: The auditors are wrong — precision must be lower than reported.

Volume itself is a contagion vector; even at 100% precision, a category whose findings are not actionable trains reviewers to dismiss the channel. The fix is to scope the category to a smaller, higher-leverage set or default-skip it.
Developers are unprofessional and need management intervention.
Aggregate precision being 100% means the system is healthy; the developer behaviour is a separate culture problem.
explanations: Audit is fine; precision is a per-finding-correctness metric, not an actionability metric.

Correct. The topic's deeper point: trust is sensitive not only to precision but to *signal-to-actionability*. Technically-correct-but-irrelevant findings cause the same disengagement as false positives. The fix is to scope or skip.
Human-layer blame — the topic's anti-pattern.
Conflates 'precision is fine' with 'the channel is healthy'; they're different.

question: A peer says: 'Our reviewer's 32%-precision comment-accuracy category is fine — we just need to ask Claude to *also* output a confidence score, then filter findings below 0.85, and we'll have an effectively precise reviewer without disabling anything.' Per the topic, what is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Confidence scores are not part of the Anthropic API and would require a custom fine-tune.
0.85 is too high a threshold; 0.7 would have worked.
The right move is to lower temperature alongside the confidence filter, which the peer omitted.

Self-reported LLM confidence is poorly calibrated against ground-truth correctness; a model that is confidently wrong on 65% of comment-accuracy findings will report high confidence on those same wrong findings, so the threshold filter doesn't actually filter false positives.
explanations: Confidence scores can be requested via tool schemas; API support isn't the issue.
Threshold tuning sidesteps the calibration problem.
Stacking anti-fixes doesn't make them work.

Correct. The topic's central principle: confidence isn't a calibrated axis. The model is already confidently producing the false positives, so a self-reported confidence threshold can't separate them. The fix is criteria sharpening or disable-and-iterate.

question: Your reviewer's 'potential null deref' category is at 35% precision. The team has shipped TWO fixes simultaneously: (1) added 'be conservative on null-deref' to the system prompt, (2) lowered temperature to 0.1 for the whole reviewer. Volume drops 40%; offline precision is unchanged at 35%. What does the topic predict and what should the team do?
options: Both fixes worked; the offline measurement must be flawed.

The volume drop is the predicted no-op of vague hedges plus temperature changes — neither touches the criterion. Disable the null-deref category in production, sharpen its criteria offline against a labelled sample with explicit categorical scope (e.g., 'flag only when the variable is dereferenced inside a branch where its return-from-nullable origin is unchecked'), and re-enable when offline precision clears the threshold.
Roll back both fixes and try a higher temperature instead; sometimes more sampling diversity surfaces better findings.
Add a third hedge ('only flag null-deref when extremely confident') and re-measure.
explanations: Offline precision unchanged is the diagnostic; the volume drop without rate change is exactly the topic's predicted outcome.
Correct. Maps to the topic's full anti-pattern stack (vague hedge AND temperature) and prescribes the disable-and-iterate workflow with an explicit categorical replacement criterion.
Temperature isn't the problem in either direction.
Stacking hedges doesn't change the criterion.
